title: Ziusudra/Utnapishtim's ark lands in the Ararat region
place_text: Shuruppak, Iraq to Mount Ararat, Armenia/Turkey

tellings.quote: Landing in the Mount Ararat region okay of uh Armenia turkey area
O man of Shurippak, son of Ubara-Tutu.
The ship took its course to the land of Nisir.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.

plain: The claim is that the ancient Mesopotamian flood hero, called Ziusudra in one version and Utnapishtim in another, sailed his ark from his city to land in the Mount Ararat region, in today's Armenia and Turkey. The researcher of ancient civilizations Matt LaCroix tells Michels this, citing the Babylonian flood poem Atrahasis and the Epic of Gilgamesh. On the Eleventh Tablet of Gilgamesh, in E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation, Utnapishtim tells his own story and is called the 'man of Shurippak,' an ancient city in what is now Iraq. He says 'The ship took its course to the land of Nisir' and 'The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.' Nisir is a mountain with its own name. It is the Bible's Book of Genesis that has the ark rest 'upon the mountains of Ararat' (Genesis 8:4), so the Ararat landing follows Genesis, not the tablet. Ziusudra is the name the older Sumerian telling gives its flood hero, and treating him as the same man as Utnapishtim is a link the tablet alone cannot make. If true, the Mesopotamian and biblical floods would be one remembered event with one landing place.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The epic gives Uta-Napishtim as the "man of Shurippak" and says "The mountain of Nisir held the ship", a mountain of its own name, where Genesis has the ark rest "upon the mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4); placing the landing in the Ararat region follows Genesis, not the tablet. Ziusudra is the name the older Sumerian telling gives its flood hero, and joining that name to Uta-Napishtim's is an identification the tablet alone cannot make. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.
